derivations.claim: Compute the moments of each error average. Linearity gives mean zero, variance addition gives variance sigma squared over r, and independence of the effects and error blocks gives independent group means with mean mu and variance tau squared plus sigma squared over r.

The centered-sum identity and the variance of the grand mean give expected between sum of squares (k-1)(tau squared plus sigma squared over r); multiplying by r/(k-1) gives E(MSB)=sigma squared plus r tau squared.
Expanding within-group residual sums and using the error moments gives expected sum of squares (r-1)sigma squared per group, hence E(MSW)=sigma squared.
Solving the two expected-mean-square equations gives the raw method-of-moments formulas and imposes no sign constraint on the tau-squared estimate.

Let $I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $N\ge2$ be a finite model index set. For each
$i\in I$, let $(\Theta_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be a measurable parameter space, let
$\Pi_i$ be a probability measure ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it, and let
$Q_i$ be a sampling kernel for a statistical experiment
([[def-statistical-experiment]]) on one common data space
$(\mathcal Y,\mathcal A)$. Assume the experiments are dominated
([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]) by the same supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$. Fix a specified likelihood density
([[def-likelihood-density]])
$f_i:\Theta_i\times\mathcal Y\to[0,\infty]$ such that
$$Q_i(\theta,B)=\int_B f_i(\theta,y)\,\mu(dy)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A).$$
Require that each $f_i$ is jointly measurable in parameter and data; separate
likelihood versions do not imply this joint measurability. Assign prior model
weights $w_i>0$ with $\sum_iw_i=1$. The **marginal likelihood**, or **model
evidence**, at $y$ is the possibly extended value
$$m_i(y):=\int_{\Theta_i} f_i(\theta,y)\,\Pi_i(d\theta)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is the BCS-02 evidence normalizer
([[def-posterior-evidence-normalizer-and-fiberwise-update]]) specialized to a
proper model prior, and is the prior-predictive density relative to the
specified common data measure. For models $i,j$ whose evidences at $y$ are both finite and positive,
the **Bayes factor for $j$ against $i$** is
$$BF_{ji}(y):=\frac{m_j(y)}{m_i(y)}.$$
The corresponding prior model odds are $w_j/w_i$. No Bayes factor is defined
here using an arbitrarily scaled improper parameter prior.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\Pi)$ be a measure space, let $L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$
be measurable for a fixed datum $y$, and put
$Z:=\int_\Theta L_y\,d\Pi$. For a finite positive constant $c$, the set
function
$$A\longmapsto c\int_A L_y\,d\Pi$$
is a probability measure if and only if $0<Z<+\infty$ and $c=Z^{-1}$. In
particular, if $Z=0$ or $Z=+\infty$, no finite positive scaling makes the
fiberwise update a probability measure.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Let $B_0,\ldots,B_{n-1}$ be a finite partition with $\mathbb P(B_i)>0$ for every $i<n$. If $\mathbb P(A)>0$, then for every $j<n$,
$$\mathbb P(B_j\mid A)=\frac{\mathbb P(A\mid B_j)\mathbb P(B_j)}{\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A\mid B_i)\mathbb P(B_i)}.$$

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Apply [F3] to $(E,\Pi)$ and this dominated observation kernel.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $N\ge2$ be a finite model index set. For each
$i\in I$, let $(\Theta_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be a measurable parameter space, let
$\Pi_i$ be a probability measure ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it, and let
$Q_i$ be a sampling kernel for a statistical experiment
([[def-statistical-experiment]]) on one common data space
$(\mathcal Y,\mathcal A)$. Assume the experiments are dominated
([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]) by the same supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$. Fix a specified likelihood density
([[def-likelihood-density]])
$f_i:\Theta_i\times\mathcal Y\to[0,\infty]$ such that
$$Q_i(\theta,B)=\int_B f_i(\theta,y)\,\mu(dy)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A).$$
Require that each $f_i$ is jointly measurable in parameter and data; separate
likelihood versions do not imply this joint measurability. Assign prior model
weights $w_i>0$ with $\sum_iw_i=1$. The **marginal likelihood**, or **model
evidence**, at $y$ is the possibly extended value
$$m_i(y):=\int_{\Theta_i} f_i(\theta,y)\,\Pi_i(d\theta)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is the BCS-02 evidence normalizer
([[def-posterior-evidence-normalizer-and-fiberwise-update]]) specialized to a
proper model prior, and is the prior-predictive density relative to the
specified common data measure. For models $i,j$ whose evidences at $y$ are both finite and positive,
the **Bayes factor for $j$ against $i$** is
$$BF_{ji}(y):=\frac{m_j(y)}{m_i(y)}.$$
The corresponding prior model odds are $w_j/w_i$. No Bayes factor is defined
here using an arbitrarily scaled improper parameter prior.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, let $\Pi$ be a
sigma-finite measure on it, and fix a data value $y$. Let
$L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ be a $\mathcal T$-measurable function. Define its
**evidence normalizer** by
$$Z_\Pi(y):=\int_\Theta L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Only when $0<Z_\Pi(y)<+\infty$ define the **fiberwise posterior update** by
$$\Pi_y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)}{Z_\Pi(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The definition makes no quotient at zero or infinite evidence. A prior is
**proper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=1$, as in
[[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. We call a sigma-finite
prior **improper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=+\infty$; the formula also applies to
other sigma-finite measures. For an improper prior, $Z_\Pi(y)$ is a fiberwise
normalizer only; it does not by itself define a prior-predictive probability or
a conditional law.

When the data are described by a dominated experiment, the dominating measure
and its sigma-finiteness are as in
[[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. A family of pointwise likelihood
sections is not assumed to be jointly measurable in parameter and data; that
additional condition must be supplied separately whenever Tonelli is used.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

citations.quote:
Fix a finite group count $m\ge1$, a standard Borel hyperparameter space
$(H,\mathcal H)$, and a standard Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$.
Let $\Pi$ be a probability measure on $(H,\mathcal H)$ and let
$$G:H\times\mathcal T\to[0,1]$$
be a probability kernel. For each $j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, let
$(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ be a measurable observation space, let $\nu_j$
be a sigma-finite measure on it, and let $K_j$ be a probability kernel from
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ with a specified
jointly measurable density $f_j:\Theta\times\mathcal Y_j\to[0,\infty]$:
$$K_j(\theta,B)=\int_B f_j(\theta,y_j)\,\nu_j(dy_j)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$

The **finite-group hierarchical model** is the following specified kernel
construction. First draw $\eta\sim\Pi$. Conditional on $\eta$, draw
$\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m$ from the finite product kernel
$$G_\eta^{\otimes m}(d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\bigotimes_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j).$$
Thus the group parameters are conditionally independent and have the same
conditional law $G_\eta$. Conditional on the parameter tuple, draw the group
observations from the product kernel $\bigotimes_{j=1}^mK_j(\theta_j,\cdot)$.
The product-kernel laws are probability kernels by
[[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]]. For each fixed $\eta$, the
coordinate maps under $G_\eta^{\otimes m}$ are independent random elements,
so their joint law is the finite product law
([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

Put $\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$ with its finite product sigma-algebra. The proper
latent prior $P_0$ on $\Xi$ is
$$P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\Pi(d\eta)\prod_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j),$$
well-defined by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. For
$\xi=(\eta,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m)\in\Xi$, lift each observation kernel
to the common source $\Xi$ by
$$M_j(\xi,B)=K_j(\theta_j,B)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$
The coordinate projection $\xi\mapsto\theta_j$ is measurable, so the kernel
definition shows that each $M_j$ is a probability kernel. Its specified
jointly measurable density is $(\xi,y_j)\mapsto f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$, by
composition with the same measurable coordinate projection. Let
$\mathcal Y=\prod_{j=1}^m\mathcal Y_j$,
$\nu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\nu_j$, and $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)$. The observation
kernel from $\Xi$ has jointly measurable density
$$L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)=\prod_{j=1}^m f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$$
with respect to $\nu$, by [[lem-finite-products-of-dominated-kernels-have-product-density]].
Its **evidence** is the possibly extended nonnegative number
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)\,P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$
The normalized likelihood measure is called a pointwise joint posterior on a
fiber only when $0<Z(y)<\infty$; no quotient is formed at zero or infinite
evidence.

For each group, $\theta\mapsto K_j(\theta,\cdot)$ is a parametric statistical
model in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], with its
parameter-measurable kernel representation as in
[[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]. Here
“conditionally independent given $\eta$” is shorthand for the explicit
finite product-kernel specification above. The library's random-element
conditional-independence terminology is defined in
[[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]; its
conditional-expectation-class convention assumes AC. The finite
product-kernel definition here does not use that class convention or any
choice axiom.

Assume the finite-group hierarchical model of
[[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]]. Write $P_0$ for its proper prior on
$\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$, let $L_y(\xi)$ be its specified product likelihood
density with respect to the finite product measure $\nu$, and define
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi).$$
For every observation $y$ with $0<Z(y)<\infty$, the measure
$$P_y(A)=\frac{\int_A L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi)}{Z(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal H\otimes\mathcal T^{\otimes m})$$
is the joint posterior law of the latent tuple. Defining $P_y=P_0$ when
$Z(y)=0$ or $Z(y)=\infty$ gives a regular conditional distribution under the
prior-predictive law; no quotient is formed on either exceptional fiber.

Assume a finite-group hierarchy as in
[[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]], with hyperparameter $\eta\in H$, group
parameters $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m$, conditional probability kernel
$G_\eta$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) on the group-parameter
space, and specified jointly measurable
likelihood density
$$L_y(\theta_{1:m})=\prod_{j=1}^m f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$$
against the common product data measure. For fixed $\eta$, define its
**marginal likelihood**
$$m(y\mid\eta):=\int_{\Theta^m}L_y(\theta_{1:m})\,G_\eta^{\otimes m}(d\theta_{1:m})\in[0,\infty].$$
Where the function $\eta\mapsto m(y\mid\eta)$ is finite-valued and attains a
positive finite maximum, a **Type-II maximum marginal likelihood choice** is
any
$$\widehat\eta(y)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\eta\in H}m(y\mid\eta).$$
This definition does not assert that a maximum exists. A data-indexed choice
requires a selected measurable maximizer on its domain.

Only when $0<m(y\mid\widehat\eta(y))<\infty$ define the corresponding
**empirical-Bayes plug-in posterior** on a measurable
$A\subseteq\Theta^m$ by
$$\Pi_{\widehat\eta(y),y}(A):=\frac{\int_A L_y(\theta_{1:m})\,G_{\widehat\eta(y)}^{\otimes m}(d\theta_{1:m})}{m(y\mid\widehat\eta(y))}.$$
The finite-positive condition makes this a probability update by
[[prop-fiberwise-posterior-propriety-iff-finite-positive-evidence]].

Under a proper hyperprior $H_0$, at a data fiber with finite positive joint evidence
$0<Z(y):=\int_Hm(y\mid\eta)H_0(d\eta)<\infty$, full Bayes instead retains the posterior law of
$\eta$ jointly with the group parameters, as in
[[thm-hierarchical-posterior-normalization-on-positive-finite-evidence]].
Integrating over a shared uncertain hyperparameter can induce dependence
between group parameters, while a plug-in update fixes that hyperparameter at
one selected value; special cases can leave the groups independent. This
definition asserts no generic empirical-Bayes risk, consistency, dominance,
or credible-coverage guarantee.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.
